name: Road trips
tagline: The high roads, driven at the right speed
summary: The Himalaya has some of the highest motorable roads in the world: Manali to Leh, the Spiti circuit, Sela Pass, the Old Silk Route. We plan them with acclimatisation days, a driver who knows the bends and honest drive times.
intro: A mountain road is slow. Two hundred kilometres can take eight hours when the road climbs over a pass, crosses snow-melt streams and waits for a landslide to be cleared. We plan drives in daylight, keep long days to one in three, and build a spare day into any route that crosses a pass above 4,000 m.

Saver road trips use state buses and shared jeeps where they run reliably. Comfort and Signature trips use a private SUV with a driver who has worked the route for years. Every road trip page lists the season the road is open, which changes year to year, so check current status before you travel.

name: Treks and walks
tagline: From an afternoon ridge walk to two weeks on foot
summary: Day walks between villages, teahouse treks in Nepal, camping treks to high lakes and passes. We grade every walk by hours, height gain and the highest point, and pair you with licensed local guides and porters where the rules or the terrain call for them.
intro: Trekking in the Himalaya is mostly walking on old paths between villages, which means you can choose your comfort: teahouses in Nepal, homestays in Ladakh and Sikkim, tents where nobody lives.

We grade honestly. A walk that gains 900 m in a day at 3,500 m is hard for anyone, fit or not, because the air is thin. Our itineraries follow the usual advice of sleeping no more than 300 to 500 m higher each night above 3,000 m, with rest days. Talk to your doctor before any high trek.

name: Monasteries
tagline: Gompas, dzongs and the mornings they keep
summary: Ladakh, Spiti, Sikkim, Bhutan, Arunachal and the Nepal Himalaya hold some of the oldest Buddhist monasteries still in use. We time visits to morning prayers and festival days, and explain the murals, masks and rules of each house.
intro: A monastery visit is best at its own hours. Most gompas hold morning prayers between 6 and 8 am, when lamps are lit and the hall fills with chant. Arrive then and you see a working house rather than a museum.
Rules vary. Some halls allow no photographs, some ask you to walk clockwise only, and some close inner shrines to women or to visitors. Our guides know each one and keep the visit respectful.

name: Pilgrimages
tagline: Char Dham, Hemkund, Muktinath and the high shrines
summary: The Himalaya is sacred ground for Hindus, Buddhists and Sikhs. We plan the Char Dham Yatra, Hemkund Sahib, Muktinath and monastery circuits with registrations, helicopter or pony options and honest notes on altitude and crowds.
intro: Pilgrim routes are crowded in their short seasons and almost empty outside them. Kedarnath and Badrinath open in late April or May and close around Diwali, on dates fixed each year by the temple committees, so check current status before you travel.

We plan pilgrimages for every budget: shared jeeps and dharamshalas, private cars and GMVN rest houses, or helicopters and the best hotels. Older pilgrims get rest days and pony or palki options where they exist.

name: Wildlife and birds
tagline: Snow leopards, red pandas and black-necked cranes
summary: Winter snow leopard trips in Ladakh and Spiti, red pandas in Singalila, cranes in Bhutan's Phobjikha and Arunachal, hornbills in Namdapha and the birding ridges of Kumaon. Timed to the season, with trackers who live there.
intro: Mountain wildlife is shy and seasonal. Snow leopards come down to lower valleys in February and March, cranes arrive in Phobjikha around late October, and the Kumaon forests are loudest with birds in spring.
We use local trackers and naturalists, and say plainly that sightings are never guaranteed.

name: Snow and winter
tagline: Gulmarg powder, Auli slopes and white Spiti
summary: Skiing in Gulmarg and Auli, winter Spiti at minus twenty, frozen Ladakh and snowfall weekends in Shimla and Manali. We plan winter trips with heated rooms, road-status checks and spare days for snow.
intro: Winter shrinks the Himalaya to the places a road still reaches. Gulmarg gets some of the deepest snow in the range from January to March. Spiti stays open from Shimla through Kinnaur when most passes close.
Winter trips need flexibility. Roads close after heavy snow and flights to Leh are cancelled in bad weather, so we keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

name: Honeymoons
tagline: Quiet rooms with the mountains outside
summary: Honeymoons in Kashmir houseboats, Bhutan's valleys, Himachal orchards and Sikkim's hills, from saver homestays to the best lodges. Slow days, good rooms, no rush.
intro: The best mountain honeymoons are slow: two or three bases, not seven, and rooms worth staying in. We avoid back-to-back long drives and add a day with nothing planned.
Budgets vary widely, and the Himalaya suits all of them. A week in Kashmir on a houseboat and in a Gulmarg hotel costs a fraction of a week in Bhutan's lodges, and both work.

name: Family holidays
tagline: Short drives, low altitudes, room to run
summary: Family trips that keep drives short and sleeping altitudes sensible: Kumaon lakes, Shimla and the toy train, Darjeeling, Gangtok, Paro and Thimphu. With notes on what children and grandparents can manage.
intro: With children and grandparents, altitude and drive time matter most. We keep most nights below 2,500 m, drives under five hours, and add at least one day without a car.
Toy trains, boats on Naini Lake, tea gardens and monastery masks hold attention far better than viewpoints.

name: Homestays and villages
summary: Homestays are the Himalaya's best value and its best way in: Ladakhi kitchens, Spiti mud houses, Kumaoni stone homes, Lepcha villages in Dzongu, Apatani homes in Ziro. Simple rooms, home food, money that stays in the valley.
intro: A homestay is a room in a family home, with meals from the family kitchen. Expect clean, simple rooms, often a shared or outside bathroom in the high valleys, and food made from what the village grows.
Many Himalayan states register homestays and some run training schemes for owners. We use registered homes where they exist and pay the family directly.

name: Food and tea
tagline: Wazwan, momos, thukpa and first flush
summary: Food trips through the Himalaya: Kashmiri wazwan, Ladakhi skyu, Himachali dham, Garhwali mandua, Newari feasts, Darjeeling tea tastings and Bhutan's ema datshi. Cheap, filling and the fastest way into a culture.
intro: Mountain food is built on what grows high and keeps through winter: barley, buckwheat, millet, potatoes, dried cheese and meat, apricots and walnuts.
Food is also where saver travellers win: a full thali or plate of momos costs little everywhere in the range.

name: Festivals
tagline: Masked dances, fairs and harvest days
summary: Tshechus in Bhutan, Hemis in Ladakh, Losar across the Buddhist Himalaya, Kullu Dussehra, Ziro's music festival and the Black-necked Crane festival. Planned around lunar dates that move every year.
intro: Most Himalayan festivals follow lunar calendars, so their dates move by weeks from year to year. We confirm dates with monasteries and organisers before you book, and you should check current status before you travel.
Festival days fill rooms early. Book three to six months ahead for Paro Tshechu and Hemis, and earlier still for the best hotels.

name: Photography
tagline: Light, height and the right hour
summary: Trips built around light: first sun on Khangchendzonga from Pelling, star skies over Chandratal and Hanle, prayer halls at dawn, apricot blossom in April. With notes on where photography is not allowed.
intro: Mountain light changes fast. The best of it is the first and last hour, which means early starts and evenings without a long drive.
Many prayer halls ban photography inside, and drones need permission almost everywhere in the Himalaya. We list the rules for each place, so check current status before you travel.

name: Adventure sports
tagline: Paragliding, rafting, skiing and high passes on two wheels
summary: Paragliding at Bir Billing, rafting on the Ganga at Rishikesh, skiing at Gulmarg and Auli, motorbike trips over Ladakh's passes. With certified operators and honest notes on season and risk.
intro: Adventure sports are regulated differently in each state. We use operators who hold the licences their state requires, and we tell you what insurance to carry.
Season matters: rafting stops in the monsoon, paragliding pauses in July and August, and skiing depends on snow.

name: Wellness and yoga
tagline: Rishikesh mornings and hot spring afternoons
summary: Yoga in Rishikesh, meditation courses in McLeodganj, hot springs at Manikaran, Gasa and Yumthang, and slow stays in forest retreats from Binsar to Bhutan.
intro: Rishikesh calls itself the yoga capital of the world and hosts the International Yoga Festival each March. Courses run from one morning class to month-long teacher trainings.
Wellness in the mountains is also simpler: hot springs, forest walks, early nights and food without much oil.
